items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Out of all the males – people – men in my life, Joe Williams was the closest person, I think, in my life, as a male – men friends.

ctx.x: There was something special about your relationship with Joe Williams.

Yes it was. It was like brothers. It was a personal relationship. We loved each other like brothers. He would call me, no matter where he was, every day at 5 o’clock. That’s martini time. That’s when we have a drink. Out of all the males – people – men in my life, Joe Williams was the closest person, I think, in my life, as a male – men friends. I didn’t have many friends. I had a lot of acquaintances and people that I dealt with. Cannonball and Joe Williams were the two people – the two main people that were my…

items.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: And I knew Joe, for years I’d known Joe Williams. And when he left the Basie band and he called me one day he said, “come and take this telephone out of my hands.”

ctx.x: That was the time when Basie finally broke up and had the six pieces, you know, because it was really rough out there for big bands. But groups like George was really hot, and Dave Brubeck, and that was the hottest things going, playing the colleges and you know, so it was really — the big band it just cost too much to travel. And the economics of it at that time was even worse than they are now. I mean they’re bad enough now, but for a big band it was terrible, you know. But anyway, that’s how I got into that…

business. And then one by one different people came along. And I knew Joe, for years I’d known Joe Williams. And when he left the Basie band and he called me one day he said, “come and take this telephone out of my hands.”
